title: Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods

concept.text: The proposed innovation is mechanical energy storage that combines low cost, useful scale, long service life, and high efficiency after extended storage, while substantially expanding where economical systems can be installed. Mechanical storage holds energy in physical states such as rotation, raised masses, or compressed fluids, then converts it back into useful output. The breakthrough target is a demonstrated combination of performance and deployment advantages; perfect efficiency and zero loss over years are unnecessary.

As an engineering synthesis, the central distinction is between an effective storage component and an effective complete installation. A system must retain energy during the waiting period, charge and discharge efficiently, and limit the electricity consumed by supporting equipment. It must also provide useful capacity and power at an acceptable site, with affordable construction, containment, maintenance, and replacement. Improvements in one component would qualify only if they produce a substantial advantage at the system level.

significance.text: Conditionally, achieving this combination could make storage economical for applications currently constrained by installation cost, location, storage duration, or standby consumption. Affordable capacity that remains useful after long waiting periods could allow energy to be shifted across longer supply gaps, while durability could reduce replacement requirements. These are consequences of the proposed capability, not demonstrated benefits of a system identified in the supplied evidence.

The potentially revolutionary change would be a large expansion in accessible, economically useful mechanical storage. The research identifies pumped storage and flywheels as existing approaches, so the innovation does not depend on treating mechanical storage itself as new. Its importance would depend on how much a demonstrated system improves on contemporary alternatives for particular applications.

As a downstream possibility, better storage could support greater use of variable electricity generation and improve flexibility in some power systems. It would not alone establish a fully renewable grid, remove transmission and integration requirements, or guarantee superiority to batteries. Applications value power, duration, efficiency, location, and response differently; a transformative advantage in one setting need not transfer to all others.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is a complete mechanical storage installation that simultaneously delivers economical capacity, useful power, durability, high efficiency over long holding periods, and materially broader deployment options. The supplied record does not establish through a current cross-technology comparison whether this combination remains unmet in every relevant application. The open target should therefore be evaluated against named use cases and contemporary alternatives.

As an engineering synthesis, the barriers differ by storage mechanism. Siting and civil works can constrain gravity-based installations; pressure or rotor containment can impose structural and safety requirements; limited energy density can increase space or material needs. Conversion equipment can dominate cost, while friction, aerodynamic drag, leakage, and supporting equipment can reduce delivered energy. These are candidate constraints to investigate for a selected design, rather than a verified comparative assessment of every mechanical storage family.

The research attributes a narrower example to Amiryar and Pullen: their flywheel model examines how bearing and windage losses affect standby and system performance. This illustrates why efficient charging and discharging alone do not establish efficient long-duration storage. However, the supplied review had no retained article text with which to verify the model assumptions or findings, and the attribution should not be generalized to all flywheels or all mechanical storage.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes several mechanical storage forms as already practical and frames the frontier as expanding their economical deployment. The accompanying review could not verify that broad characterization from inspectable source material. The record therefore provides background context, but no independently inspectable deployment inventory, current performance comparison, or demonstration of the proposed breakthrough.

The sole indexed publication is Mustafa E. Amiryar and Keith R. Pullen’s “Analysis of Standby Losses and Charging Cycles in Flywheel Energy Storage Systems,” dated 27 August 2020 in the supplied research. That research attributes to Sections 4–5 an analysis of bearing and aerodynamic losses and their effects on standby and round-trip performance in a modeled flywheel design. This is a design-specific modeling attribution, not a reported demonstration of inexpensive mechanical storage retaining high efficiency over multiple weeks.

The source index marks the article as not captured and contains no retained artifacts. The review consequently could not independently check its contents, modeling assumptions, or the magnitude of the reported effects. No numerical efficiency, retention, or cost values are available in the supplied material for responsible inclusion here. This evidence limitation does not show that the paper’s findings are false.

No documented freshness search was supplied to establish the field’s status as of 1 November 2026. Accordingly, neither present-day openness of the proposed capability nor a current cross-technology cost benchmark can be established from this record. The dated flywheel analysis also does not establish that the proposed system-level combination is achievable.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a grid-connected mechanical storage installation, or one at comparably relevant scale and operating conditions, for a clearly named application. Independently measure charging energy, usable discharged energy, capacity, power, and performance over both daily and multiweek holding periods. Repeat the operating cycles sufficiently to characterize consistency and emerging degradation. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Relevant-scale mechanical storage performance measured across daily and multiweek holds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement boundaries: report charging and discharging losses, energy retained during storage, and auxiliary consumption separately, alongside an explicitly defined overall round-trip efficiency. Specify whether supporting equipment draws power from the stored energy or an external supply, and include that consumption in the complete energy accounting. Report operating conditions, measurement uncertainty, and changes in usable capacity so that a favorable conversion-efficiency figure cannot obscure poor retention or substantial standby demand.
completion_criteria.label: Round-trip efficiency reported with complete energy accounting and uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic test: choose a contemporaneous, application-matched baseline before testing and define the cost and efficiency improvements that would count as substantial. Distinguish installed capital cost from lifecycle cost, and disclose assumptions about utilization, maintenance, replacement, service life, and energy losses. A credible claim of lower lifecycle cost should show how measured performance supports the calculation and how uncertain assumptions affect the result.
completion_criteria.label: Cost and efficiency improvements evaluated against a predefined application-matched baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the operating protocol, energy accounting, uncertainty analysis, and sufficient design information available for independent assessment and repeat testing. Report containment requirements, footprint, site dependence, maintenance, and degradation. Tests across multiple holding times and operating conditions would establish the breadth actually demonstrated; they would not establish universal superiority across sites, storage mechanisms, or grid applications.
completion_criteria.label: Independent repeat testing enabled and practical deployment limits reported

related_concepts.text: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” overlap with the management of friction and contact losses in storage machinery. MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” overlaps with maintenance planning and reliable lifecycle estimates. These concepts address contact behavior and component longevity; MEC-14 requires a favorable complete storage system even if those component advances become available.

MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” could conditionally improve repeatedly loaded structures, rotors, or containment. Their targets concern material capabilities. Stronger or more fatigue-resistant components would not by themselves establish economical storage, low standby consumption, or broad siting flexibility.

MEC-01, “An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow,” could overlap with predicting aerodynamic or fluid losses where those effects matter. MEC-03, “Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting,” has a more conditional connection through thermal management or recovery of low-temperature heat in suitable system designs. Neither concept is equivalent to storing mechanical energy efficiently over long periods, and neither is established here as a prerequisite.

MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” overlaps with designing machinery that meets multiple constraints. MEC-14 is narrower in application and more demanding in measured operational and economic outcomes: producing a feasible mechanism does not establish a competitive storage installation. These roster relationships are conceptual synthesis, not evidence of demonstrated dependencies between the innovations.

unresolved_issues: The indexed 2020 article has no retained text or artifacts, leaving its detailed assumptions and findings unverified within the supplied record.
No current cross-technology evidence establishes which applications already meet parts or all of the proposed capability.
The target application, storage mechanism, capacity, power, holding period, and acceptable site requirements remain unspecified.
Numerical cost, efficiency, retention, durability, and improvement thresholds remain to be chosen against an application-matched baseline; none can be established from the supplied evidence.
No demonstrated installation or independently reproduced result in the supplied material establishes that the full proposed combination is achievable.

brief.title: Affordable energy storage that lasts for weeks
possible: Electricity suppliers could save energy for weeks and recover most of it when needed, using affordable equipment that lasts and can be installed in more places.
These systems would store energy in motion, raised weights or compressed fluids. The goal is a complete installation that combines low cost, useful output and low losses throughout the wait.
why: Affordable storage over long periods could help electricity suppliers bridge longer gaps in supply. Durable equipment could also reduce replacement needs.
More places could use economical storage, helping power systems accommodate changing wind and solar output.

sources.who: Mustafa E. Amiryar and Keith R. Pullen
sources.showed: This is a modeling study of how bearing friction and air resistance affect energy losses in a flywheel, which stores energy in a spinning rotor.
sources.cited_for: It addresses energy lost while a flywheel waits and during charging and discharge.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an affordable complete installation that retains high efficiency over weeks.

sources.who: Emeric Dormoy, Brice Le Lostec and Didier Haillot
sources.showed: They combined experiments with a model of aboveground compressed-air storage. Heating the air before expansion and adding turbine stages improved the predicted share of energy recovered.
sources.quote: Experimental data calibration ensured model accuracy with a mean absolute percentage error below 4.0%
sources.cited_for: It shows how design choices affect energy recovery in aboveground compressed-air storage.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate low cost, long service life and high energy recovery after weeks of storage together.

shown: Emeric Dormoy and colleagues used experimental measurements to calibrate a model of aboveground compressed-air storage. Their analysis predicted energy recovery of up to 16% with preheating and added turbine stages. This was a model result, not a demonstration of efficient storage over weeks.
missing: A complete installation has yet to demonstrate affordable capacity, useful power, long life and high energy recovery after weeks together.
The combined advantage still needs to extend to practical sites, including construction, containment, maintenance and space requirements.
Measured performance still needs to support lower lifetime costs against alternatives serving the same application.

milestones.label: Useful-scale performance across daily and multiweek storage
milestones.explanation: Repeated tests would have to measure energy in and out, capacity and power at a scale relevant to a named use. This would establish whether performance survives long waits and repeated operation.

milestones.label: Energy recovery measured with every loss included
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to include charging, waiting, discharge and supporting equipment, with uncertainty reported. This would establish how much usable energy the whole installation returns.

milestones.label: Cost and efficiency gains against a chosen alternative
milestones.explanation: Measured performance would have to support predefined cost and efficiency gains against an alternative chosen for the same use. This would test whether the advantage holds over the installation's life.

milestones.label: Repeatable tests and clear deployment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent repeat testing would have to be enabled by shared methods and sufficient design details, with practical limits reported. This would establish where the demonstrated performance applies.

uncertain: The intended application, storage method, scale and acceptable site requirements remain unspecified.
The cost, efficiency and durability thresholds that would count as success remain to be chosen.
Which applications already achieve the proposed combination, and how much room remains for improvement, is unresolved.

page.title: Long-duration mechanical electricity storage
page.definition: Mechanical electricity storage meets ARPA-E’s DAYS cost, duration and siting targets. It holds energy in compressed fluids or raised masses and converts that energy back into electricity.

goal.need: DOE’s 2024 technology comparison places pumped hydro and compressed air in the discharge-duration and cost ranges below. DAYS seeks 10–100-hour discharge without dependence on site-specific geology. The comparison gives technology-level ranges; these are not audited installation costs or measurements of energy retention during weeks idle.

figures.caption: Mechanical-storage characteristics reproduced in DOE’s 2024 pilot funding notice.
figures.note: Source: Figure 2. These ranges use the source’s cost conventions and should not be treated as calculations under the DAYS protocol.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy
statements.quote: DAYS projects will explore a new design space in electricity storage
statements.context: DAYS means Duration Addition to electricitY Storage. The announcement includes mechanical approaches.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Electricity
statements.quote: Long-duration (10+ hours) energy storage technologies are needed to support a variety of clean energy and resilience applications.

completion.title: A mechanical electricity-storage system meets the DAYS cost, duration and siting targets.
completion.criterion: A mechanical electricity-in/electricity-out system meets DAYS Table 1: ≥100 kW peak output; 10 to approximately 100 h rated discharge; no reliance on site-specific geologic structures; and LCOS ≤US$0.05/kWh-cycle across that duration range. Use Equation 1, Figure 2B’s daily-plus or non-daily duty cycle, US$0.025/kWh charging electricity, a 10% discount rate and a 20-year lifetime. Include capital, maintenance, replacements and inefficiency. LCOS is the storage cost adder, excluding the purchase cost of electricity ultimately delivered.
completion.set_by: ARPA-E, DAYS Program Overview, Section 3, Table 1, Equation 1 and Figure 2B.
completion.threshold_quote: The principal target metric of the DAYS program is an LCOS of 5 cents/kWh-cycle.
completion.basis: DAYS explicitly includes mechanical systems and combines cost, duration and siting requirements. Its expectation of greater than 50% round-trip efficiency is not a separate mandatory threshold. Discharge duration does not establish energy retention after weeks idle.

milestones.title: Laboratory experiments validate a mechanical-storage concept’s critical functions against predictions.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE technology readiness level (TRL) 3: analytical studies and laboratory experiments physically validate critical functions; complete-system integration is not required. Dormoy and colleagues’ paper, published 1 December 2024, calibrates an aboveground compressed-air model against experiments with mean absolute percentage error below 4%; its 4.5–16.0% round-trip efficiencies are model results. Amiryar and Pullen’s paper, published 27 August 2020, models flywheel bearing and aerodynamic losses.
milestones.set_by: DOE Office of Electricity, Energy Storage Structured Technology Review Laboratory Call, Appendix 1, TRL-3 row; criterion appears only in a table.

milestones.title: An engineering-scale mechanical-storage prototype performs its functions in a relevant environment.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE TRL 6: test an engineering-scale prototype capable of all functions required of the operational system, in an environment closely representing actual operation. Related field evidence is Quidnet’s announcement on 26 February 2025 of MWh-scale functional and accelerated lifetime testing at its Greater Houston site. This company result is not peer reviewed and is not a DOE TRL assessment.
milestones.set_by: DOE Office of Electricity, Energy Storage Structured Technology Review Laboratory Call, Appendix 1, TRL-6 row; criterion appears only in a table.

milestones.title: A mechanical-storage pilot delivers at least 1 MW AC continuously for at least 10 hours.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate at least 10 continuous hours of discharge at or above 1 MW AC, using a commercially relevant module or minimum unit size, and attain integrated-system TRL 7–8. These are DOE’s default mechanical-storage pilot requirements under DE-FOA-0003399; the notice permits applicants to justify departures from its size or duration requirements. The pilot benchmark does not establish the DAYS lifetime-cost target.
milestones.set_by: DOE Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, DE-FOA-0003399, Technology and System Requirements, Table 2 and accompanying text.
milestones.threshold_quote: All projects are expected to attain at least 10 hours of continuous discharge at or above the minimum capacity.

milestones.title: A complete mechanical-storage system passes qualification tests in its final form under expected conditions.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE TRL 8: complete the actual system and qualify it through testing and demonstration in its final form under expected conditions. Related announcements concern one plant per example: Nant de Drance pumped hydro, 900 MW, commissioned 1 July 2022; Zhangjiakou compressed air, 100 MW, grid-connected 30 September 2022; and Rudong solid-mass gravity, 25 MW/100 MWh, with units tested and commissioning reported on 4 May 2024. These announcements are not peer reviewed and do not constitute DOE TRL assessments.
milestones.set_by: DOE Office of Electricity, Energy Storage Structured Technology Review Laboratory Call, Appendix 1, TRL-8 row; criterion appears only in a table.

not_found: Searches of ARPA-E DAYS, DOE Storage Shot and DOE pilot criteria found no joint numerical threshold for efficiency after a multiweek idle hold, lifetime cost and unrestricted siting.
Searches for mechanical-storage demonstrations meeting the DAYS cost target found no full-scale result establishing all programme metrics under its specified duty cycle.
The opened Dormoy abstract gives no experimental sample size, and the Quidnet release gives no cycle count or numerical round-trip efficiency.
The opened plant announcements do not report the controlled continuous-discharge test specified in milestone m3.

results.finding: Aboveground compressed-air model, sample size not stated: experimental calibration produced mean absolute percentage error below 4.0%.
results.detail: The reported 4.5–16.0% round-trip efficiencies are results of parametric modeling.
results.quote: Experimental data calibration ensured model accuracy with a mean absolute percentage error below 4.0%

results.finding: One 1.5 MW SustainX compressed-air prototype operated in charge and discharge modes.
results.detail: The prototype was grid-connected at Seabrook, New Hampshire, but initial testing used load banks to prevent energy from being fed back to the grid. The text does not establish that all functions required of the operational system were tested.
results.quote:
The 1.5 MW Commercial Prototype has been operational for both compressions (charge) and expansions (discharge) 
since September 30, 2013.

results.finding: One Jintan compressed-air storage system passed four full-load charge-discharge cycles.
results.detail: The 60 MW system passed a full-load trial before commercial operation and later completed overall performance testing. The source does not report a formal DOE TRL assessment.
results.quote: 通过连续完成满负荷“4充4放”验证机组安全可靠性的技术标准，经过充分准备后储能电站一次性顺利通过测试。

results.finding: One Nant de Drance pumped-storage plant, rated 900 MW, completed commissioning and on-site testing.
results.detail: Commissioning tests validated operating behavior and safety limits. Delayed load rejection tests used conservative head conditions; the paper does not report a DOE TRL assessment.
results.quote:
The commissioning of the Nant de Drance pumped 
storage power plant (PSP ) was recently completed in the heart 
of the Swiss Alps . This latter is equipped with six reversible 
variable speed pump-turbines corresponding to a total power of 
900 MW.

results.finding: One heat-transfer test stand achieved 95% isothermal efficiency in a spray-assisted expansion.
results.detail: The experiment compared actual expansion work with theoretical isothermal work and physically demonstrated a critical heat-transfer function.
results.quote:
When the same mass of air was expanded again, this time with the water spray, the 
temperature curved back up towards the theoretical once the spray started (at approximately 0.5 
seconds into the expansion) and maintained a 15°C difference with ambient for the remainder of the 
stroke, achieving a 95% isothermal efficiency.

results.detail: The report states the prototype's rated scale but does not demonstrate continuous discharge at or above 1 MW AC for 10 hours or establish TRL 7–8.

results.finding: One Jintan compressed-air system completed full-load testing before commercial operation in 2022.
results.detail: The integrated 60 MW system stores compressed air in a salt cavern and generates electricity for the grid. Its full-load test and subsequent operation demonstrate the required functions in an operational environment.

results.finding: One Jintan compressed-air system achieved its 5-hour generation design condition.
results.detail: The system is rated at 60 MW, but the reported generation period is five hours, short of the required 10 continuous hours. The source does not report a DOE TRL assessment.
